about: What stood in Nuʻuanu, Honolulu and the neighbouring valleys, with the battles of 1783 and 1795 as masses and lines. DATA.md “District packs” gives the schema; RESEARCH.md §10 says how each feature was made. A feature’s to year is the last year a source read shows it, not a sourced end. Forces and lines carry event, when and step (their order within the event); heiau carry placePrecision and ahupuaa and stand at the ahupuaʻa centroid; ponds from the State site record carry its site number.

properties.name: Loʻi of Nuʻuanu
properties.note: The valley floor along Nuʻuanu Stream from the mouth of the valley to about Kahapaʻakai. Kamakau describes the old road from Kahapaʻakai down the valley as running between villages and garden patches of taro, sweet potato, bananas, ʻawa, wauke, sugarcane and olonā; Ellis, in the early 1820s, walked from the valley mouth through one unbroken series of irrigated plantations. The outline is drawn, not mapped: gentle ground near the stream below the valley sides, from the island heights and the stream layer, checked against the ruled valley floor of the 1881 sheet. The kuleana awards that would map the patches themselves are not in the digitised award layer for Honolulu. The end year is the last map read that shows the ground as wet land.

properties.name: Upland loʻi of Nuʻuanu
properties.note: The flats of Luakaha and Makuku above Kahapaʻakai. Kamakau says that when all the lands below were under cultivation Kamehameha, in his years on Oʻahu, carried cultivation up Nuʻuanu as far as Keawawapuʻahanui, and he has Boki growing taro from Kahapaʻakai to Makuku in 1829. Whether these uplands were in taro before the conquest is not said, so the patches begin the year after it. Outline drawn as for the lower valley.

properties.name: Loʻi of Pauoa
properties.note: The floor of Pauoa along its stream, which the 1881 sheet rules as wet land. No source read describes Pauoa’s patches in 1795; Kamakau names the Pauoa stream on the old road and Pauoa in the battle of 1783. Outline drawn as for Nuʻuanu.

properties.name: Loʻi of Kapālama
properties.note: Along Kapālama Stream. Kamakau names Kapālama among the lands Kamehameha cleared and planted in his years on Oʻahu; whether it was all in loʻi in 1795 is not said. Outline drawn as for Nuʻuanu.

properties.name: Loʻi of Kapālama
properties.note: Along Kapālama Stream. Kamakau names Kapālama among the lands Kamehameha cleared and planted in his years on Oʻahu; whether it was all in loʻi in 1795 is not said. Outline drawn as for Nuʻuanu.

properties.name: Loʻi of Kalihi
properties.note: The floor of Kalihi Valley along its stream. The few Kalihi awards in the digitised layer lie in the upper valley and carry no land use; the outline is drawn as for Nuʻuanu and checked against the 1881 sheet. The district box cuts the head of the valley.

properties.name: Loʻi of Mānoa
properties.note: The broad floor of Mānoa along Mānoa and Waihī streams, ruled as wet land on the 1881 sheet. No source read describes Mānoa’s patches in 1795. Outline drawn as for Nuʻuanu.

properties.name: Loko Kuwili
properties.note: One of the ponds of Kālia on the Waikīkī shore, outlined in the State historic site record as the Kīpuka layer publishes it. The 1881 sheet rules this shore as wet land; the 1899 sheet still draws ponds at Kālia; the 1927 sheet shows them filled. When the pond was built is not in any source read. Spelling as the site record gives it, for a speaker to check.

properties.name: Ananoho
properties.note: The site record calls this Kalihi Fishponds; its outline is the pond the 1927 sheet names Ananoho. The 1881 sheet writes the land names Apili, Pahounui, Kaluapulu and Mokauea along this shore. When the pond was built is not in any source read; spelling as printed in 1927, for a speaker to check.

properties.name: Pahouiki
properties.note: The site record names it with Pahounui and Apili; its outline is the pond the 1927 sheet names Pahouiki. When the pond was built is not in any source read; spelling as printed in 1927, for a speaker to check.

properties.name: Apili
properties.note: Traced from the 1927 sheet, which names the pond; the site record groups the Kalihi ponds under two numbers. When the pond was built is not in any source read; spelling as printed in 1927, for a speaker to check.

properties.name: Pahou

properties.name: Kuwili
properties.note: The 1881 sheet writes Kuwili on the harbour shore west of Iwilei and rules the low ground behind it as wet land; the 1899 sheet keeps the name by the railway depot, and the 1927 sheet shows the ground filled. No source read outlines the ponds, so this shape only marks where they were.

properties.name: Kahoʻikekanaka
properties.note: Kamakau names the fishponds of Kahoʻikekanaka makai of Honuakaha, fed by a watercourse from Kaʻakopua, in his account of Honolulu in Liholiho’s time. Nothing read places them more closely; the shape is a marker on the old shore below Honuakaha.

properties.name: Kou
properties.note: The village at the harbour, between the mouth of Nuʻuanu Stream (Kikihale) and Pākākā, from the shore inland about as far as King Street runs today. Kamakau’s account of Liholiho’s Honolulu, about 1820, runs from the Kikihale stream to Honuakaha; in 1795 the village was smaller, and its bounds are not recorded, so the outline is inferred. By the 1820s Kamakau and Ellis describe a town here, which the near view should draw instead.

tellings.says: No count of houses. Honolulu “was seldom used in Ka-lani-ku-pule’s day”; in Kamehameha’s time the chief lived half the time at Waikīkī and half in Honolulu, and Liholiho made it his usual residence, with houses from above the Kikihale stream down to Kapuʻukolo and on to Honuakaha (pp. 271–272).

In the early 1820s the town, grown with the shipping, “usually” held “6000 or 7000 inhabitants” (p. 17). No source read gives a count of households at Kou in 1795; they were fewer than this, and no estimate is offered here.

properties.name: Kaheiki
properties.note: A heiau of the class Thrum calls pookanaka, said to be of Menehune building; Thrum lists its site as undiscovered. In 1783 Kahahana’s defence stood behind it, and Kamakau names its guardian stone Hoʻeu by the stream of Kaheiki. Shown only as within Honolulu ahupuaʻa.

properties.name: Pākākā
properties.note: The heiau of Pākākā at the harbour of Kou, pookanaka in Thrum’s list, its site not located. Shown only as within Honolulu ahupuaʻa; the place Pākākā is in the gazetteer as the landing, not the heiau.

properties.name: Kawaluna
properties.note: A luakini at Waolani in Nuʻuanu, consecrated by Kualiʻi in Thrum’s list; tradition puts the first heiau of Oʻahu at the entrance to Waolani. Kamakau says many celebrated heiau stood between Kahapaʻakai and the mouth of the valley. Shown only as within Honolulu ahupuaʻa.

properties.name: Makuku
properties.note: A heiau to bring rain in upper Nuʻuanu, its site not located (Thrum). Shown only as within Honolulu ahupuaʻa.

properties.name: Kaahaimauli
properties.note: In Thrum’s list at the site of the Executive Building, its size and kind unknown by then. Spelling as Thrum prints it, for a speaker to check. Shown only as within Honolulu ahupuaʻa.

properties.name: Nuʻuanu Stream
properties.note: The modern course from the State stream layer, joined straight across the reservoirs where the layer has no line. The lower reach is channelled today, and the mouth at Kou lay on the old shore, not the modern wharves.

properties.name: Pauoa Stream
properties.note: The modern course from the State stream layer; it joins Nuʻuanu Stream above the harbour.

properties.name: Waolani Stream
properties.note: The modern course from the State stream layer.

properties.name: Kapālama Stream
properties.note: The modern course from the State stream layer; its lower reach is a drainage canal today.

properties.name: Kalihi Stream
properties.note: The modern course from the State stream layer; the district box cuts the head of the valley.

properties.name: Mānoa Stream
properties.note: The modern course from the State stream layer, up the Waihī branch; below the valley it now runs into the Ala Wai canal, dug in the twentieth century, so the reach below the valley mouth is left out.

properties.name: The way up Nuʻuanu
properties.note: From Kou up the valley to the gap at the pali. Ellis walked it in the early 1820s through plantations and then thickets of hibiscus to the pass; Kamakau describes the old road from Kahapaʻakai down the valley through villages and gardens, overgrown with hau near the mouth until Keanini cleared and widened it to haul timber over the pali for Kawaiahaʻo, about 1828. The line is the road of the 1881 sheet as today’s streets keep it (Nuʻuanu Avenue, the Pali Highway and Nuʻuanu Pali Drive); no source read says the older path ran exactly here.

properties.name: The path down the pali
properties.note: Ellis climbed the pali from Koʻolau by a path that rose steeply in two places near the top, where people passed with heavy loads; stone figures stood on either side of the path at the head of the pass, and are not placed. The line only gives the direction of the descent to the windward foot.

properties.name: Kaʻiana’s people cross from Koʻolau
properties.note: Kaʻiana and those who went with him leave the fleet in the channel, land on the Koʻolau side and cross the mountain to join Kalanikūpule. Fornander says only that they crossed; the pass at the head of Nuʻuanu is the obvious way, but no source names it. How many went is not recorded.

properties.name: Kalanikūpule’s posts up the valley
properties.note: Kalanikūpule holds the valley at a chain of named places, from Puʻiwa at the bottom upward through Kaumuʻohena, Kapaʻeli, Kaukahōkū, Kawānanakoa, Luakaha, Kahapaʻakai and Kanoneakapueo to the head of the valley; Fornander gives that order, Kamakau the same names from the top down. Only Puʻiwa, Lāʻimi and Luakaha are placed from a map; the line stands for the chain, not for positions.

properties.name: Kamehameha’s army ashore from Waiʻalae to Waikīkī
properties.note: The fleet lands and the army comes ashore along the beaches from Waiʻalae to Waikīkī, and spends a few days putting itself in order. The coast round Lēʻahi lies outside the district, so the line runs behind it.

properties.name: The march past Kou and up the valley
properties.note: The sources say only that the army marched up Nuʻuanu from the landing. The line crosses the plain past Kou and follows the valley road to the foot of Puʻiwa; an oral account brings most of the army from Kāhala and Kaimukī straight to the foot of Pūowaina instead.

properties.name: The Oʻahu line falls back to Lāʻimi
properties.note: After the fighting at Puʻiwa the Oʻahu side gives ground, and at Lāʻimi it is routed. The order of the two places is Kamakau’s.

properties.name: The retreat to the head of the valley
properties.note: The rest of the Oʻahu forces fall back up the valley to the pali, where the land drops away to Koʻolau. What happened at the edge is told differently in every source, and is a burial matter; nothing is drawn there.

properties.name: The pursuit up the valley
properties.note: Kamehameha’s forces follow the retreat up the valley; Fornander has Kalanikūpule hotly pursued.

properties.name: Over the ridge into Kalihi
properties.note: Fornander: of those not killed, some escaped up the sides of the mountains that enclose the valley. An oral account says most went over ʻĀlewa into Kalihi and on toward ʻAiea. The line gives the direction only.

properties.name: Up the eastern side of the valley
properties.note: Escape up the eastern side of the valley, toward Pauoa, which Fornander allows; the oral account has some go up Pacific Heights, while Kamehameha’s riflemen fire from Pauoa Flats above. The line gives the direction only.

properties.name: Down the old path to Koʻolau
properties.note: Only the oral account says that many of those who reached the head of the valley got away down the old paths on the pali; Ellis describes the path. The line shows people going down the path, not over the edge.

properties.name: The Oʻahu line at Puʻiwa
properties.note: Where the fighting begins, at the lowest of the Oʻahu posts. For a while it is hotly contested (Fornander). The ends of the line are schematic; the sources give the place, not the front.

properties.name: Kamehameha’s front at Puʻiwa
properties.note: Kamehameha’s guns, more of them and better served, turn the day (Fornander, who names no gunner). Jarves, the 1911 Annual and Johnstone put John Young at a gun; no source read puts Isaac Davis at Nuʻuanu. The ends of the line are schematic; the sources give the place, not the front.

properties.name: The Oʻahu line breaks at Lāʻimi
properties.note: At Lāʻimi the Oʻahu side is routed and Kaʻiana falls, in Kamakau’s telling; the other tellings place his death elsewhere (see the event). The ends of the line are schematic; the sources give the place, not the front.

properties.name: Kamehameha’s front at Lāʻimi
properties.note: The advance that breaks the Oʻahu line. The ends of the line are schematic; the sources give the place, not the front.

properties.name: Kahekili’s column by Pūowaina
properties.note: Fornander has Kahekili march from Waikīkī in three columns, by Pūowaina, Pauoa and Kapena; Kamakau has two companies, one under Hueu at Kanelaʻau and Kapapakōlea behind Pūowaina. The line gives the direction only.

properties.name: Kahekili’s column by Pauoa
properties.note: The column by Pauoa, up to the ridge between Pauoa and Nuʻuanu. The line gives the direction only.

properties.name: Kahekili’s column by Kapena
properties.note: The column by Kapena, round the town side of Pūowaina to Nuʻuanu Stream; Kamakau has Kahekili’s own company stationed from above Hekili to Kahehuna and ʻAuwaiolimu. The line gives the direction only.

properties.name: Kahahana’s defence at Kaheiki
properties.note: The defence stationed behind the heiau of Kaheiki, attacked on the ridge facing Pauoa and from there down to Kapena (Kamakau). It breaks, and Kahahana and his wife Kekuapoʻi flee to the mountains. The heiau itself is not placed.
